overview.title: Going further with LLMs: from supervised fine-tuning to RLHF
overview.main_topic: Why supervised fine-tuning is limited, and how RLHF uses human preference rankings to train a reward model that then supervises the LLM through reinforcement learning.
overview.central_idea: Handwritten responses are slow, expensive and capped at human performance; what we really want to optimize is human preference. RLHF starts from supervised fine-tuning, trains a reward model on human rankings of responses, and then improves the LLM by letting it learn from rewards on its own generated outputs.
overview.importance: RLHF is the step that turned pretrained LLMs into products like ChatGPT; this page lays out its rationale and stages.
learning_objectives: Define supervised fine-tuning and explain why it is called supervised.
List the limitations of manually written training responses.
Explain why human preference is hard to turn into a differentiable loss.
Describe how a reward model is built from ranked responses and what it outputs.
Explain reinforcement learning in terms of actions and rewards.

summary:
Section **16.4 Going further with LLMs** opens by noting that we have trained a GPT model from scratch and fine-tuned a language model into a chatbot, but this only scratches the surface. The section will cover a non-exhaustive list of extensions to the basic "autocomplete the internet" setup.

**16.4.1 RLHF.** The instruction tuning just performed is called **supervised fine-tuning** (SFT): supervised because we curate, by hand, the prompts and responses we want. Manual data has two problems: it is a **bottleneck** (slow and expensive), and it is limited by the **human performance ceiling**. To exceed human performance in a chatbot, we cannot rely on manually written outputs.

The real objective is our **preference** for some responses over others. With enough people this is perfectly well defined, but translating "our preferences" into a loss we can compute gradients of is tricky. **Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF)** addresses this.

The recipe: (1) start with SFT on handwritten prompts and responses as a baseline. (2) Build a **reward model** as a proxy for human preference: gather many prompts and candidate responses (handwritten, generated by the model, or by other chatbots), and have human evaluators **rank** the responses for each prompt from most to least helpful. This is slow and expensive but faster than writing all the desired responses. (3) Train the reward model on this ranked dataset: it takes a **prompt-response pair** and outputs **a single float**, higher meaning better; it is usually **another, smaller Transformer** that reads the whole sequence instead of predicting the next token. (4) Use the reward model to tune the LLM with **reinforcement learning**, which the authors define broadly as any setup where a model learns by making predictions (**actions**) and receiving feedback on them (**rewards**). In short, the model's own predictions become its training data. The concrete loop follows on p.520.

concepts.name: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
concepts.significance: First stage of RLHF; gives a good baseline.
concepts.misconception: That it can surpass the quality of its demonstrations; it is limited by the human ceiling.

concepts.name: Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF)
concepts.definition: Training an LLM to maximize a reward model learned from human preference rankings, on top of SFT.
concepts.intuition: Instead of showing the model perfect answers, a judge (trained on human tastes) scores its attempts and it learns to please the judge.
concepts.technical: SFT → collect rankings → train reward model (prompt+response → float) → RL optimization of the LLM against the reward.
concepts.significance: Used to turn GPT-3 into ChatGPT (p.520).
concepts.example: Evaluators rank four responses to a prompt; the reward model learns to score the top one highest.
concepts.misconception: That humans score every training sample during RL; they only label the reward model's data.

concepts.name: Reward model
concepts.definition: A model, usually a smaller Transformer, mapping a prompt-response pair to a single float that proxies human preference.
concepts.intuition: An automated critic trained to agree with human raters.
concepts.technical: Sequence-to-scalar regression; trained on ranked responses.
concepts.example: Score 2.3 for a helpful answer, -1.1 for an unhelpful one.
concepts.misconception: That it predicts next tokens; it outputs one rating per sequence.

concepts.name: Reinforcement learning (broad sense)
concepts.definition: Any training setup where a model learns from feedback (rewards) on its own predictions (actions).
concepts.intuition: Learning by trial and feedback, not by copying answers.
concepts.technical: Policy = the LLM; action = a generated response; reward = reward model score.
concepts.significance: Lets a model's own outputs become training data.
concepts.misconception: That RL requires games or robots; the book stresses it is a general training setup.

deeper.title: Why ranking beats writing
deeper.body: Writing an excellent answer to a hard question requires expertise; recognizing the better of two answers often does not. Rankings are therefore cheaper per example and can reflect quality levels the raters could not produce themselves, which is how RLHF can push past the human performance ceiling the book mentions.

deeper.title: How rankings become a loss (beyond the book)
deeper.body:
1. Expand each ranking of K responses into K(K−1)/2 pairs (preferred $y_w$, rejected $y_l$).
2. Score both with the reward model $r$.
3. Minimize $-\log \sigma\bigl(r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l)\bigr)$, which pushes the preferred score up relative to the rejected one.
4. Only score differences matter, so the reward is defined up to a constant. This is the formulation used by Ouyang et al. (2022), cited on p.520.

deeper.title: Restaurant critic analogy
deeper.body: SFT is a cook copying recipes from a cookbook. RLHF hires a panel to taste dishes and rank them, trains a critic to predict the panel's verdict, and then lets the cook experiment endlessly with the critic's feedback. The cook can end up better than the cookbook authors.

takeaways: Instruction tuning on curated examples is called supervised fine-tuning (SFT).
Manual examples are a bottleneck and cap performance at human level.
The true objective is human preference, which is hard to express as a differentiable loss.
RLHF: SFT baseline → human rankings of responses → reward model (prompt+response → float, usually a smaller Transformer) → RL tuning.
Reinforcement learning = learning from rewards on one's own actions; the model's predictions become its training data.

questions.question: Why is the Dolly-style instruction tuning called 'supervised'?
options: Because a reward model supervises it
Because humans curate the example prompts and responses by hand
Because a teacher model distills into it
questions.answer: Because humans curate the example prompts and responses by hand
questions.explanation: Stated on the page. Reward models belong to RLHF; images and distillation are unrelated here.

questions.question: Name two limitations of manually written training responses given on the page.
questions.answer: They are slow and expensive (a bottleneck), and they limit the model to the human performance ceiling.
questions.explanation: Both are stated in the paragraph beginning 'Any need to manually write…'.

questions.question: What does the reward model output?
options: A single floating-point value for a prompt-response pair
questions.answer: A single floating-point value for a prompt-response pair
questions.explanation: The page says it outputs a single float; higher is better. Rankings are its training data, not its output.

questions.question: Why is it easier to collect rankings than desired responses?
questions.answer: Judging which of several existing responses is most helpful is faster and cheaper than writing the ideal response from scratch.
questions.explanation: The page says ranking is expensive and slow but still faster than writing all desired responses.

questions.question: In the book's description of reinforcement learning, what are 'actions' and 'rewards' for an LLM?
questions.answer: Actions are the model's generated responses; rewards are the reward model's scores of those responses.
questions.explanation: Defined on this page and made concrete on p.520.

questions.question: Why is human preference hard to use directly as a training loss?
questions.answer: Preferences are judgments made by people, not differentiable functions of the model's outputs, so you cannot compute gradients from them directly; a learned reward model provides a proxy.
questions.explanation: The page calls translating preferences into a loss 'quite tricky'; the reward model is the proxy.

questions.question: Can you list the four stages of RLHF in order without looking?
questions.answer: SFT; collect and rank responses; train reward model; RL tuning against the reward model.
